ann_17.original: The model's age effect is a rising line with a ceiling. Through its own edge (in the direct terms) age adds 0.81 to the score per standard deviation. This part is a single hinge on age that switches on for the oldest patients: the unit grows by 0.96 per standard deviation of age (and by -0.085 per standard deviation of creatinine, a small shift of the threshold) and feeds the score with weight -0.91, which cancels the direct age term, so above the turn the predicted risk is flat. Self-probe (age sweep at the typical case, creatinine 85 µmol/L): risk 1% at age 20, 15% at 60, 41% at 80 (hinge still off, unit value 0.00), then 41% at 85 (hinge on, value 0.38) and 40% at 95: the turn lies between ages 80 and 85 years at that creatinine. Higher creatinine raises the age threshold a little: at age 85 the unit is 0.52 at creatinine 40 and 0.00 at 220 µmol/L; switching the creatinine edge off changes the risk of 85 training patients, by at most 0.059. On the training data the hinge is on for 76 of 1500 patients (outcome rate 61.8%, mean predicted risk 63%), for 0 patients under 80 years and for 36 of the 36 aged 85 or more. Switching the part off: over the 76 patients it acts on, its mean effect on predicted risk is -0.050 (risk with the part minus risk without), at most 0.25 for one patient; whole-model AUC 0.8458 with it and 0.8447 without. Concept probe: age alone predicts the gate with score 1.00. Clinically: the model's risk rises with age up to the early eighties and then stops rising. The regime is small (76 rows) and may be fitted to those rows.
ann_17.proposed: A hinge for cases older than about 77 years that lowers their predicted risk a little, softening the age effect.

ann_18.original: A serial chain of hinges on one load index: blood pressure and heart rate rising together. The first unit (node 534) sums systolic pressure (weight 1.92 per standard deviation) and heart rate (1.42 per standard deviation) and is on for 963 of 1500 training patients; node 1197 is an always-on linear copy of it (weight 1.16); the second stage (node 2442, weight 1.05 from the first unit, a higher threshold) is on for 419; the third (node 7124) for 224; the fourth (node 7602) for 73 (a small regime, outcome rate 12.3%, mean predicted risk 14%). Each stage feeds the score with a negative weight (-0.20, -0.63, -0.54, -0.51, -0.63 per unit), so the chain is a decreasing, convex penalty: the more stages are on, the steeper the fall in the score as pressure and rate rise together. Turning points at the typical case: with systolic 133 mmHg the first stage switches on between heart rates 65 and 70 beats/min (unit 0.11), the second between 85 and 90, the third between 95 and 100, the fourth between 110 and 115; with heart rate 76 beats/min the first stage switches on between systolic 125 and 130 mmHg, the second between 145 and 150, the third between 155 and 160, the fourth between 170 and 175. The side unit (node 560) adds systolic pressure (0.97 per standard deviation) to the second stage (1.00), is on for 527 patients, and passes mainly to the rate-bmi amplifier (edge weight 0.336); its own edge to the score (-0.024) moves a patient's risk by at most 0.033 when switched off, and fixing the unit at zero changes AUC from 0.8458 to 0.8414. Whole-part ablation (exits at baseline): AUC 0.8458 with, 0.7258 without; over the 419 patients with the second stage on, the part's mean effect on predicted risk is -0.427 (with minus without), and over the 963 with the first stage on it is -0.178. Concept probe: the sum systolic pressure + heart rate predicts the gates with score 0.95; the rate-pressure product (systolic pressure times heart rate, a clinical index of myocardial oxygen demand) scores 0.90. Clinically: this part lowers the predicted risk when blood pressure and heart rate are both high, and the more so the higher they are together; it is what makes the model's risk fall again in the both-high corner of the pressure-rate plane (see the root).
ann_18.proposed: A load that lowers the predicted risk when systolic pressure and heart rate are high together, starting above about 126 mmHg of systolic pressure for a typical case.

ann_19.original: A hinge on the contrast between systolic blood pressure and heart rate: the unit (node 440) grows by 1.13 per standard deviation of systolic pressure and changes by -0.91 per standard deviation of heart rate, so it is on when pressure is high for the heart rate. It is on for 790 of 1500 training patients (outcome rate 42.9%, mean predicted risk 43%). It adds to the score directly with weight 1.13 per unit and feeds the rate-bmi amplifier with weight 1.21. Turning points at the typical case: with systolic 133 mmHg the unit is 0.20 at heart rate 75 and 0.00 at 80 beats/min; with heart rate 76 beats/min it is 0.00 at systolic 130 and 0.25 at 135 mmHg. Self-probe at a slow heart rate (55 beats/min): raising systolic pressure from 90 to 160 mmHg takes the unit from 0.00 to 3.27 and the whole-model risk from 3% to 92%. Switching the part off: over the 790 patients where it acts, its mean effect on predicted risk is 0.313 (with minus without); whole-model AUC 0.8458 with and 0.6658 without, the largest loss of any part. Concept probe: the difference systolic pressure minus heart rate (raw units) predicts the gate with score 1.00; the ratio of pressure to rate scores 0.98. Clinically: a high systolic pressure with a slow heart rate (a wide pressure-rate gap) raises the predicted risk steeply; a fast heart rate at the same pressure switches this part off.
ann_19.proposed: A hinge that raises the predicted risk when systolic pressure is high for the heart rate, from about 131 mmHg for a typical case.

ann_21.original: Two nearly linear hinges in series. The first (node 2391) sums bmi (0.34 per standard deviation), heart rate (0.77 per standard deviation) and the pressure-over-rate unit (weight 1.21 per unit, through an identity entry); the second (node 1686) takes the first with weight 1.14, adds the load chain's side unit scaled by 0.336, and feeds the score with weight 0.93. The first hinge is on for 1271 and the second for 1157 of 1500 training patients (outcome rate 44.0% and mean predicted risk 45% when on). Where on, the part is a positive, close to linear term in bmi, heart rate and the pressure-rate contrast. Self-probe (bmi sweep at the typical case): the exit is 0.00 at bmi 26 and 0.16 at 28 kg/m²; whole-model risk is 15% at bmi 16 and 15% at 26, then rises to 33% at 40 and 44% at 46. The direct bmi edge is 0.0013 per standard deviation, so the model's bmi effect runs through this part: flat at low bmi, rising above the turn, whose position depends on heart rate and pressure. At systolic 110 mmHg the exit is 0.00 at heart rate 70 and 2.26 at 110 beats/min, carrying part of the model's heart-rate effect at low pressure. The side signal matters little: switching its edge off changes AUC from 0.8458 to 0.8409 (1239 patients affected, max risk change 0.37). Whole-part ablation: AUC 0.8458 with, 0.7825 without; over the 1157 patients where it acts its mean effect on predicted risk is 0.187 (with minus without). ann_22.original: The linear part of the model. Each input adds its edge weight per standard deviation to the score (inputs are standardised; the weights are not per raw unit): heart rate 1.29, age 0.81, creatinine 0.46, smoker 0.45, diabetes 0.43, male 0.21, systolic pressure 0.077, bmi 0.0013. Smoking, diabetes and male sex each raise the score by a fixed amount (one-hot inputs, standardised); creatinine raises it linearly over its whole range (at age 85 the whole-model risk is 22% at creatinine 40 and 85% at 190 µmol/L); age's direct term is the rising line that the age ceiling flattens above the early eighties. Heart rate's direct term is the largest but is opposed by the load chain and by the pressure-over-rate hinge, so the whole-model heart-rate effect is not this weight: at systolic 110 mmHg risk rises with heart rate from 3% to 90% (40 to 110 beats/min), while at systolic 150 it falls from 89% to below 1% (see the root). Switching the direct edges off (each replaced by its mean contribution): AUC 0.8458 with, 0.6764 without; mean absolute risk change 0.21. Concept probe: a weighted sum of heart rate, age and creatinine (the sum's own three largest terms) scores 0.82; heart rate alone scores 0.51. This part is described by its formula (a linear risk score) rather than by a single clinical concept.

ann_23.original: The predicted risk is a sigmoid of a sum of the five parts: the direct terms, plus the pressure-over-rate hinge, plus the rate-bmi amplifier (which is itself fed by the pressure-over-rate hinge and, weakly, by the load chain's side unit), minus the pressure-rate load chain, minus the age ceiling. The nonlinear parts matter: linearising every hidden unit lowers the training AUC from 0.8458 to 0.7450. By AUC without the part: pressure-over-rate 0.6658, direct terms 0.6764, load chain 0.7258, amplifier 0.7825, age ceiling 0.8447. The main joint effect is a saddle in systolic pressure and heart rate: the pressure-over-rate hinge raises risk when pressure is high for the heart rate; the direct heart-rate term and the amplifier raise it when the heart rate is high; the load chain pulls it down, ever more steeply, when pressure and rate are high together. So the heart-rate effect reverses with pressure: at systolic 110 mmHg risk rises with heart rate from 3% at 40 beats/min to 90% at 110; at systolic 150 it falls from 89% to below 1% over the same range; at systolic 180 it falls from above 99% to 9% by 80 beats/min. Likewise the pressure effect reverses with heart rate: at heart rate 55 risk rises with systolic pressure from 3% at 90 mmHg to 97% at 180, while at heart rate 95 it falls from 85% to 3% at 150 mmHg. The training data show the same four corners: systolic 150 or more with heart rate 65 or less, 61 patients, outcome rate 90.2%, mean predicted risk 89%; systolic 115 or less with heart rate 90 or more, 46 patients, 76.1%, 70%; both high (150 or more, 90 or more), 38 patients, 5.3%, 4%; both low (115 or less, 65 or less), 57 patients, 1.8%, 8%. At the typical case the single-input curves are therefore non-monotone: heart rate 35% at 40, 16% at 80, 26% at 100, 5% at 130 beats/min; systolic 21% at 90, 17% at 130, 39% at 160, 6% at 200 mmHg. Age: risk rises from 1% at age 20 to 41% at 80, then is flat (40% at 95) because the age ceiling cancels the direct term. Bmi: flat up to about 26 kg/m² then rising, through the amplifier. Creatinine, smoking, diabetes and male sex: positive direct terms. Sodium and noise are not connected to the output: sweeping sodium from 120 to 155 mmol/L leaves the typical case's risk at 17% and 17%, and noise from -3 to 3 at 17% and 17%. The annotated model reproduces the evolved network: max absolute output error 4.4e-16 over 1500 training rows.
ann_23.proposed: The model adds up five parts on one score: a pressure and heart rate load, a hinge for pressure that is high for the heart rate, direct terms, a heart rate and BMI amplifier and an age ceiling; systolic pressure and heart rate form a saddle, and the model ignores serum sodium and the random noise column.

parts.name: risk_score
parts.original_hypothesis: The predicted risk is a sigmoid of a sum of the five parts: the direct terms, plus the pressure-over-rate hinge, plus the rate-bmi amplifier (which is itself fed by the pressure-over-rate hinge and, weakly, by the load chain's side unit), minus the pressure-rate load chain, minus the age ceiling. The nonlinear parts matter: linearising every hidden unit lowers the training AUC from 0.8458 to 0.7450. By AUC without the part: pressure-over-rate 0.6658, direct terms 0.6764, load chain 0.7258, amplifier 0.7825, age ceiling 0.8447. The main joint effect is a saddle in systolic pressure and heart rate: the pressure-over-rate hinge raises risk when pressure is high for the heart rate; the direct heart-rate term and the amplifier raise it when the heart rate is high; the load chain pulls it down, ever more steeply, when pressure and rate are high together. So the heart-rate effect reverses with pressure: at systolic 110 mmHg risk rises with heart rate from 3% at 40 beats/min to 90% at 110; at systolic 150 it falls from 89% to below 1% over the same range; at systolic 180 it falls from above 99% to 9% by 80 beats/min. Likewise the pressure effect reverses with heart rate: at heart rate 55 risk rises with systolic pressure from 3% at 90 mmHg to 97% at 180, while at heart rate 95 it falls from 85% to 3% at 150 mmHg. The training data show the same four corners: systolic 150 or more with heart rate 65 or less, 61 patients, outcome rate 90.2%, mean predicted risk 89%; systolic 115 or less with heart rate 90 or more, 46 patients, 76.1%, 70%; both high (150 or more, 90 or more), 38 patients, 5.3%, 4%; both low (115 or less, 65 or less), 57 patients, 1.8%, 8%. At the typical case the single-input curves are therefore non-monotone: heart rate 35% at 40, 16% at 80, 26% at 100, 5% at 130 beats/min; systolic 21% at 90, 17% at 130, 39% at 160, 6% at 200 mmHg. Age: risk rises from 1% at age 20 to 41% at 80, then is flat (40% at 95) because the age ceiling cancels the direct term. Bmi: flat up to about 26 kg/m² then rising, through the amplifier. Creatinine, smoking, diabetes and male sex: positive direct terms. Sodium and noise are not connected to the output: sweeping sodium from 120 to 155 mmol/L leaves the typical case's risk at 17% and 17%, and noise from -3 to 3 at 17% and 17%. The annotated model reproduces the evolved network: max absolute output error 4.4e-16 over 1500 training rows.

parts.name: pressure_rate_load
parts.original_hypothesis: A serial chain of hinges on one load index: blood pressure and heart rate rising together. The first unit (node 534) sums systolic pressure (weight 1.92 per standard deviation) and heart rate (1.42 per standard deviation) and is on for 963 of 1500 training patients; node 1197 is an always-on linear copy of it (weight 1.16); the second stage (node 2442, weight 1.05 from the first unit, a higher threshold) is on for 419; the third (node 7124) for 224; the fourth (node 7602) for 73 (a small regime, outcome rate 12.3%, mean predicted risk 14%). Each stage feeds the score with a negative weight (-0.20, -0.63, -0.54, -0.51, -0.63 per unit), so the chain is a decreasing, convex penalty: the more stages are on, the steeper the fall in the score as pressure and rate rise together. Turning points at the typical case: with systolic 133 mmHg the first stage switches on between heart rates 65 and 70 beats/min (unit 0.11), the second between 85 and 90, the third between 95 and 100, the fourth between 110 and 115; with heart rate 76 beats/min the first stage switches on between systolic 125 and 130 mmHg, the second between 145 and 150, the third between 155 and 160, the fourth between 170 and 175. The side unit (node 560) adds systolic pressure (0.97 per standard deviation) to the second stage (1.00), is on for 527 patients, and passes mainly to the rate-bmi amplifier (edge weight 0.336); its own edge to the score (-0.024) moves a patient's risk by at most 0.033 when switched off, and fixing the unit at zero changes AUC from 0.8458 to 0.8414. Whole-part ablation (exits at baseline): AUC 0.8458 with, 0.7258 without; over the 419 patients with the second stage on, the part's mean effect on predicted risk is -0.427 (with minus without), and over the 963 with the first stage on it is -0.178. Concept probe: the sum systolic pressure + heart rate predicts the gates with score 0.95; the rate-pressure product (systolic pressure times heart rate, a clinical index of myocardial oxygen demand) scores 0.90. Clinically: this part lowers the predicted risk when blood pressure and heart rate are both high, and the more so the higher they are together; it is what makes the model's risk fall again in the both-high corner of the pressure-rate plane (see the root).

parts.name: pressure_over_rate
parts.original_hypothesis: A hinge on the contrast between systolic blood pressure and heart rate: the unit (node 440) grows by 1.13 per standard deviation of systolic pressure and changes by -0.91 per standard deviation of heart rate, so it is on when pressure is high for the heart rate. It is on for 790 of 1500 training patients (outcome rate 42.9%, mean predicted risk 43%). It adds to the score directly with weight 1.13 per unit and feeds the rate-bmi amplifier with weight 1.21. Turning points at the typical case: with systolic 133 mmHg the unit is 0.20 at heart rate 75 and 0.00 at 80 beats/min; with heart rate 76 beats/min it is 0.00 at systolic 130 and 0.25 at 135 mmHg. Self-probe at a slow heart rate (55 beats/min): raising systolic pressure from 90 to 160 mmHg takes the unit from 0.00 to 3.27 and the whole-model risk from 3% to 92%. Switching the part off: over the 790 patients where it acts, its mean effect on predicted risk is 0.313 (with minus without); whole-model AUC 0.8458 with and 0.6658 without, the largest loss of any part. Concept probe: the difference systolic pressure minus heart rate (raw units) predicts the gate with score 1.00; the ratio of pressure to rate scores 0.98. Clinically: a high systolic pressure with a slow heart rate (a wide pressure-rate gap) raises the predicted risk steeply; a fast heart rate at the same pressure switches this part off.

parts.name: direct_terms
parts.original_hypothesis: The linear part of the model. Each input adds its edge weight per standard deviation to the score (inputs are standardised; the weights are not per raw unit): heart rate 1.29, age 0.81, creatinine 0.46, smoker 0.45, diabetes 0.43, male 0.21, systolic pressure 0.077, bmi 0.0013. Smoking, diabetes and male sex each raise the score by a fixed amount (one-hot inputs, standardised); creatinine raises it linearly over its whole range (at age 85 the whole-model risk is 22% at creatinine 40 and 85% at 190 µmol/L); age's direct term is the rising line that the age ceiling flattens above the early eighties. Heart rate's direct term is the largest but is opposed by the load chain and by the pressure-over-rate hinge, so the whole-model heart-rate effect is not this weight: at systolic 110 mmHg risk rises with heart rate from 3% to 90% (40 to 110 beats/min), while at systolic 150 it falls from 89% to below 1% (see the root). Switching the direct edges off (each replaced by its mean contribution): AUC 0.8458 with, 0.6764 without; mean absolute risk change 0.21. Concept probe: a weighted sum of heart rate, age and creatinine (the sum's own three largest terms) scores 0.82; heart rate alone scores 0.51. This part is described by its formula (a linear risk score) rather than by a single clinical concept.

parts.name: rate_bmi_amplifier
parts.original_hypothesis: Two nearly linear hinges in series. The first (node 2391) sums bmi (0.34 per standard deviation), heart rate (0.77 per standard deviation) and the pressure-over-rate unit (weight 1.21 per unit, through an identity entry); the second (node 1686) takes the first with weight 1.14, adds the load chain's side unit scaled by 0.336, and feeds the score with weight 0.93. The first hinge is on for 1271 and the second for 1157 of 1500 training patients (outcome rate 44.0% and mean predicted risk 45% when on). Where on, the part is a positive, close to linear term in bmi, heart rate and the pressure-rate contrast. Self-probe (bmi sweep at the typical case): the exit is 0.00 at bmi 26 and 0.16 at 28 kg/m²; whole-model risk is 15% at bmi 16 and 15% at 26, then rises to 33% at 40 and 44% at 46. The direct bmi edge is 0.0013 per standard deviation, so the model's bmi effect runs through this part: flat at low bmi, rising above the turn, whose position depends on heart rate and pressure. At systolic 110 mmHg the exit is 0.00 at heart rate 70 and 2.26 at 110 beats/min, carrying part of the model's heart-rate effect at low pressure. The side signal matters little: switching its edge off changes AUC from 0.8458 to 0.8409 (1239 patients affected, max risk change 0.37). Whole-part ablation: AUC 0.8458 with, 0.7825 without; over the 1157 patients where it acts its mean effect on predicted risk is 0.187 (with minus without). Concept probe: the sum systolic pressure + bmi + heart rate predicts the exit with score 0.84 (bmi + heart rate alone 0.61; the pressure enters through the pressure-over-rate unit), so the part is best read as a general haemodynamic-plus-body-size load rather than a single clinical concept. Clinically: higher bmi and a faster heart rate raise the predicted risk through this part, and more so when systolic pressure is high relative to the heart rate.

parts.name: age_ceiling
parts.original_hypothesis: The model's age effect is a rising line with a ceiling. Through its own edge (in the direct terms) age adds 0.81 to the score per standard deviation. This part is a single hinge on age that switches on for the oldest patients: the unit grows by 0.96 per standard deviation of age (and by -0.085 per standard deviation of creatinine, a small shift of the threshold) and feeds the score with weight -0.91, which cancels the direct age term, so above the turn the predicted risk is flat. Self-probe (age sweep at the typical case, creatinine 85 µmol/L): risk 1% at age 20, 15% at 60, 41% at 80 (hinge still off, unit value 0.00), then 41% at 85 (hinge on, value 0.38) and 40% at 95: the turn lies between ages 80 and 85 years at that creatinine. Higher creatinine raises the age threshold a little: at age 85 the unit is 0.52 at creatinine 40 and 0.00 at 220 µmol/L; switching the creatinine edge off changes the risk of 85 training patients, by at most 0.059. On the training data the hinge is on for 76 of 1500 patients (outcome rate 61.8%, mean predicted risk 63%), for 0 patients under 80 years and for 36 of the 36 aged 85 or more. Switching the part off: over the 76 patients it acts on, its mean effect on predicted risk is -0.050 (risk with the part minus risk without), at most 0.25 for one patient; whole-model AUC 0.8458 with it and 0.8447 without. Concept probe: age alone predicts the gate with score 1.00. Clinically: the model's risk rises with age up to the early eighties and then stops rising. The regime is small (76 rows) and may be fitted to those rows.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient); an input the data ties to a category takes its typical value within that category (linked inputs)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients

confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients
